rows.question: A release changed config and ran unknown migration steps. Recommend recovery actions with rollback constraints and data safety checks.
rows.answer: To recover from this partial upgrade issue, follow these steps in order: 1. **Rollback Database Migrations**: - First, identify which SQL migration scripts were executed during the upgrade. You can find this by looking at the full deployment logs or using a tool like pg_dump for PostgreSQL to capture the migration steps before and after. 2. **Stop the affected services**: - Safely halt the application components that are showing intermittent failures or errors. This prevents further damage while you address the issue. - For example, if the upgrade affected a specific feature, stop the corresponding service instances until you can fix the underlying problem. 3. **Revert to pre-upgrade state**: - Roll back your database schema to the last stable point before the unknown migration steps were executed. This ensures that your system is in a consistent state for troubleshooting. - You may need to create and restore a full backup of the affected databases, using tools like pg_dump for PostgreSQL or mysqldump for MySQL. 4. **Identify impacted users**: - Determine which users or applications were affected by the unknown migration steps. This will help you prioritize remediation efforts and identify any potential data loss or corruption. - You may need to review user behavior logs, error reports, or application monitoring dashboards to track affected customers. 5. **Re-evaluate dependencies**: - Review any external systems or services that are affected by the upgrade failure. This includes integration points with other applications and third-party services. 6. **Review system stability**: - Monitor your application's performance after reverting the database migrations. Look for any lingering issues related to the unknown migration steps. - Use application monitoring tools like New Relic, Dynatrace or AppDynamics to track performance metrics over time and identify potential issues that may have been introduced by the upgrade. 7. **Document your findings**: - Document the root cause of the issue, the affected components, and any known impact on users. This will help you understand how the unknown migration steps caused the upgrade failure. - Use a tool like Jira or Confluence to log the findings and track follow-up actions. 8. **Plan for future migrations**: - Review your team's migration strategy and make sure that it includes the use of documented migration scripts, proper rollback procedures, and monitoring tools to catch potential issues before they impact production. - Use a tool like GitLab CI/CD or Jenkins to automate your build, test, and deployment processes. 9. **Communicate with stakeholders**: - Communicate the findings of the investigation to relevant stakeholders and customers. Provide an update on the status of the incident and any planned actions to resolve the issue. - Use a tool like Slack or Microsoft Teams to share updates in real-time with your team and impacted users. 10. **Re-evaluate impact**: - Monitor the system's performance after implementing the rollback steps and the identified remediation actions. Look for any lingering issues that may have been introduced by the upgrade. - Use application monitoring tools like New Relic, Dynatrace or AppDynamics to track performance metrics over time and identify potential issues that may have been caused by the unknown migration steps. Remember, it's crucial to document your findings and keep a record of any actions taken. This will help you avoid similar incidents in the future and improve your overall system's stability.

Once you identify them, create backups of the changed environment variables and ensure that the app is using the backup versions. 5. **Recover Application Services:** - After applying the config file rollbacks, start up the affected application services one by one. - Monitor their health and performance as they come back online to ensure that everything is functioning correctly post rollback. 6. **Verify Recovery:** - Once all of the services are fully recovered, perform end-to-end tests on the application to verify that it functions correctly in its intended state. - This may involve running through your unit and integration tests, as well as performance tests to ensure that the recovery did not have any impact on the application's performance. This should bring it in line with what it was before the release went out. - Use a tool like `php migration:rollback` to execute an opposite migration for each identified script. - Or, if you have access to the source files, manually apply them in reverse order. 4. **Check for any remaining lingering changes**: After rolling back, verify that all config and schema changes are now reverted. - Look at your application's config files (e.g., `.env`, `app.yml`) to make sure they match their pre-upgrade state. - Examine the database to confirm it has been restored to its original condition. 5. **Re-test the application**: Once you've ensured that all changes are rolled back, restart the services and test your application thoroughly to ensure it is stable again. - If any intermittent failures or errors persist, investigate further using logging and monitoring tools. **Caution**: Only attempt this process in an environment where you can tolerate downtime. The rollback will be irreversible if executed on a production system with live data. Always test the rollbacks first in staging or pre-prod before applying them to prod.

Make sure to use this feature when migrating your tables and relationships. 5. Monitor Migration Progress: Keep an eye on the migration progress to ensure it is running smoothly.
